panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (R (1985), R (2010)). R (1985): Right eye IVFA from 1985 in patient with dense deposit disease showing drusen; in-text describes drusen progression between 1985 and 2010 without vascular leakage. R (2010): Right eye IVFA at re-referral in 2010 in same dense deposit disease patient showing increased number and distribution of drusen compared to 1985, no vascular leakage.
panels.attribution_text: Cunningham and Kotagiri. A long history of dense deposit disease.. BMC ophthalmology 2018. doi:10.1186/s12886-018-0853-8. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Comparison of the IVFA of the right eye at presentation in 1985 and at re-referral in 2010
in_text_mentions: lated macular degeneration, and a small area of possible sub-retinal fluid. Comparison was made between the IVFA in 1985 and the IVFA at re-referral showing a significant increase in the number and distribution of the drusen, but no vascular leakage (Fig. 3). The poor vision in the left eye was found to be secondary to advanced glaucoma and significant changes at the macula. No treatment was appropriate and the patient was monitored for 5 years with repeated Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) scans.Fig. 3Comparison of the IVFA of the right eye at presentation in 1985 and at re-referral in 2010

panels.rationale: Real patient OCT from dense deposit disease case showing drusen in Bruch's membrane with preserved RPE/photoreceptors, matching sub-RPE drusenoid deposits and juvenile subretinal drusen.
panels.attribution_text: Cunningham and Kotagiri. A long history of dense deposit disease.. BMC ophthalmology 2018. doi:10.1186/s12886-018-0853-8. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 5.
panels.figure_caption: OCT cut through drusen showing preservation of the RPE and photoreceptors, with thickening of Bruch’s membrane
in_text_mentions: At the most recent visit (October 2016) the patient’s BCVA was recorded in the right eye as 49 ETDRS letters and awareness of hand movements only in the left eye. The fundus examination demonstrated multiple subretinal drusenoid deposits, which were autofluorescent, mainly at the posterior pole. Careful review of the OCT images demonstrated that the deposits were in Bruch’s membrane, with an intact Retinal Pigment Epithelium (RPE) (Fig. 5).Fig. 5OCT cut through drusen showing preservation of the RPE and photoreceptors, with thickening of Bruch’s membrane
